Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I call to order the 6th informal meeting of the Plenary on the question of equitable representation on an increase in the membership of the Security Council and other matters related to the Council. I would like to express my sincere gratitude to all delegations for their active participation during the meetings of the IGN on 21 January. As indicated in the message circulated via e-delegate on 24 February, this meeting will be dedicated to cluster discussions on working methods. The model discussion originally scheduled for tomorrow, 28 February, will not take place. This discussion will be held in the format of an open meeting with webcast and will be followed by a closed interactive session without webcast as soon as the list of speakers in the open meeting is exhausted. Delegations were invited to inscribe on the list of speakers via eDelegate, and the live link to the list of speakers was circulated to all delegations. At this stage, if a delegation wishes to be added to the existing list of speakers, a representative should inform the Secretariat table. If a delegation wishes to speak on behalf of a group of states, a representative should inform the Secretariat in order to be given priority. Before we begin, I would like to remind members that delegations are encouraged to email a copy of their statements to eStatements for the publication on the repository website as well as to facilitate interpretation. I now give the floor to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

Thank you, co-chairs, for giving me the floor. I have the honor of delivering today's statement On behalf of the L69, a diverse, pro-reform group of 29 cross-regional developing countries united by the urgent need for comprehensive reform of the Security Council. Co-chairs, Excellencies, thank you for convening today's meeting on the Cluster of Working Methods. While we recognize the interconnectedness of the 5 clusters, we also note that the working methods of the Council would be dependent ultimately on the size of the reformed and expanded Council. However, working methods remain fundamental for the effective functioning of the Security Council in any configuration. The L69 has repeatedly emphasized that to preserve the credibility and legitimacy of the Security Council, the principles of equity and fair representation must guide our reform efforts As such, these very principles must also underpin the working methods of the Council. The informal system of penholdership, which concentrates power into the hands of a few countries, ultimately preserving the influence of old imperial powers, must be restructured. This current system has resulted in a skewed structure that favors the Global North, to the detriment of the Global South, which remains underrepresented and sidelined. To promote fairness, there must be a more inclusive mechanism that enables all Council members to play a more direct role in shaping the decisions and outcomes of the Council. Additionally, in an enlarged Council, it is imperative that non-permanent members be given the opportunity to hold the presidency of the Council at least once during their tenure. As the IGN navigates its current stalemate and explores avenues for concrete progress on reform, the Informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions remains crucial. In its current configuration, and even after reform is complete, it is this subsidiary body that would safeguard the effectiveness, transparency, efficiency, and agility of the Council. We have heard concerns that a Council that is too large can be detrimental to the efficiency of its work. However, with appropriate working methods, the Council can suitably address any potential gaps and maintain opportunities for the wider membership to contribute to its— to this process. Including by maximizing the use of existing mechanisms such as the open debate on working methods. As we are aware, the working methods of the Council require constant reflection, adaptation, and adjustment to ensure their effectiveness. The Council already has at its disposal very useful working methods that have been carefully negotiated and agreed upon. Their impact is wholly dependent their effective implementation. While the IWG is indispensable for the effectiveness of the Council, we underscore that its impact will be limited as long as the structural deficiencies in the representativeness and equity of the Council remain unaddressed. These flaws have rendered the Council incapable of fully discharging its mandate, fueling skepticism about its continued relevance in today's world. Therefore, comprehensive reform remains a vital next step. Strengthening the current working methods of the Council is not a substitute for concrete progress on reform. We recognize that reform will be transformative, catapulting us into uncharted territory. This is precisely why a review mechanism would be useful, as it offers a path to future adjustments. Thank you. One reform is that once reform is achieved, the IWG's role will be to evaluate the reformed Council and identify and address gaps to improve the functioning of an expanded Council. The debate on working methods also called for introspection of working methods of the IGN. It is time to move away from repetitive series of debates and discussions that fail to yield concrete outcomes. Actionable measures that result in tangible milestones are what we need. These may be pursued in a democratic manner, taking on board the views and concerns of L69 and the larger Global South. The very spirit of inclusivity, representativeness, and equity needs to be reflected in the functioning of this august forum as well. Co-chairs, Excellencies, The L69 will continue to engage constructively in the IGN throughout this session. We are hopeful that our inputs will be duly incorporated into the consolidated model. We underscore that such a product should neither be a mere compilation of positions nor a document with vagaries. Instead, it should be a document with actionable language that can form the basis of substantive text based negotiations in the next session. It bears reiteration that such a document may be drawn up in a democratic manner through a consultative, inclusive, and transparent process. We underline that this text will enable the commencement of real negotiations, taking us away from this cycle of repetition. It would allow us to better identify the convergences and move ahead towards achieving reforms in a time-bound manner. If member states are truly committed to reform, the negotiations would only enhance our discussions. The L69 is ready to contribute constructively to the preparation of this text and count on our colleagues to do the same. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and I give the floor to Italy.

Distinguished co-chairs, I will make this intervention on behalf of Uniting for Consensus, a diverse cross-regional pro-reform group that comprises Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Malta, Mexico, Pakistan, Republic of Korea, San Marino, Spain, Turkey, and my own country, Italy. I wish to thank you for convening this 3rd meeting of the IGN for this 79th session of the General Assembly, focusing on the working methods of a reformed Security Council. The UFC proposal stems from the understanding that any reform of the Council, and especially its enlargement, should take into thorough consideration the Council's working methods. And the impact on its ability to generate concrete outcomes. A more representative and accountable Council must also be a more efficient and transparent one. If the structure of the current Council needs to be reformed, its working methods must be equally reviewed. We must go beyond focusing solely on categories of membership and seat allocations, and follow a comprehensive and balanced approach to the reform of this body that takes into account the strong interlinkages between the 5 clusters of Decision 62/557. Flexible, inclusive and transparent decision-making processes are key aspects of any reformed and enlarged Security Council. So, how can we enhance the working methods of a reformed Council? First and foremost, the primary goal should be to promote inclusivity, efficiency, and further democratization of the Council by ensuring all elected Members play a central role in its decision-making processes. All Members of the Council must have the opportunity to participate equally in shaping the Council's agenda, drafting outcomes, engaging in consultations, and presiding over its work, order for decisions to be made jointly and transparently. Moreover, we advocate for institutionalizing a more equitable distribution of responsibilities, including the sharing of penholderships and chairships of subsidiary bodies between permanent and elected Members. We also support the adoption of inclusive working practices that ensure non-Council Members have timely a meaningful access to important documents such as draft resolutions, presidential statements, press statements, and other Security Council materials such as elements to the press and notes by the President, thereby fostering a more representative and participatory decision-making process. In addition, we propose improving the analytical quality of the Security Council's annual report ensuring that it provides a comprehensive and critical assessment of the Council's performance. The UFC advocates for measures that will boost the transparency of both the Council and its subsidiary bodies. This includes improving the availability, frequency, and quality of formal and informal reports, summary records, and briefings for non-Council members. This should also extend to strengthening collaboration with regional and sub-regional Many other improvements do not require changes to the UN Charter and can be applied to the current structure of the Council to improve its functioning. For example, increasing the involvement of elected Members in drafting resolutions and chairing subsidiary bodies is already feasible within the current framework. Distinguished Co-Chairs, the UFC also believes that the Security Council and the General Assembly must work in harmony, complementing and reinforcing each other's mandates. It is true that, due to its structure, the Security Council lacks the representativeness and democratic nature of the General Assembly, which includes all Member States. This makes it crucial to improve the Council's accountability to the broader UN membership. So, how can this be done? The answer lies in periodic elections to ensure Council members remain accountable to the General Assembly. The active involvement of elected members in Security Council decision-making is, at its core, an exercise in democracy. Adding new permanent members would diminish the Council's adaptability and further entrench exclusivity making the body less democratic and less representative. When it comes to consultations between the Council and the wider UN membership, there is a broad consensus that improvements are needed. Transparency should be considered as the cornerstone of any genuine democratic reform. Ensuring that the views and concerns of Member States directly affected by any issue under the Council's agenda are heard, and taken into account. As for enhancing cooperation between the Security Council and other UN bodies, the UFC advocates for closer collaboration with the Peacebuilding Commission. We look forward to seeing the Council regularly seek, deliberate on, and incorporate the PBC's targeted and strategic advice into its decision-making processes, particularly in the context of peacekeeping transitions and peacebuilding aspects of peacekeeping mandates, giving appropriate advance notice and timelines to the PBC to allow for the provision of timely advice to the Council. Additionally, we believe the Council should engage more consistently with multilateral and regional partners, such as the African Union's Peace and Security Council. As many African nations remind us during discussions at the IGN meetings, Much of the Security Council's agenda concerns Africa, and African states are among the largest contributors of troops and police personnel to UN peacekeeping missions. A more structured partnership between the UN Security Council and the AU's Peace and Security Council could enhance more local ownership and foster more effective responses to conflicts. Similarly, the Council should also promote cooperation with other relevant regional and cross-regional organizations. Distinguished Co-Chairs, the UFC believes that a Council enlarged with elected members will enhance its effectiveness and efficiency. For example, in the last decades, the vast majority of proposals, suggestions and practices to improve the working methods of the Security Council came from the elected members, commonly referred to as the E10. We have seen over the years many more concrete examples of how elected Members can contribute to the works of the Council, perform efficiently as innovators and bridge-builders. Distinguished Co-Chairs and colleagues, these are just some of the main ideas of the UFC regarding the cluster of working methods of a reformed Council. We look forward to continuing our constructive engagement in the discussions ahead. We remain convinced that pragmatism should lead us all when we approach an issue as delicate as the Security Council reform. We should all be ready to compromise and aim at a reform for all, in line with our times. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy. And I give the floor to Sierra Leone.

Distinguished co-chairs, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the African Union member states. We sincerely appreciate your convening of today's meeting and acknowledge your introductory remarks. Africa is grateful for your steadfast commitment to the intergovernmental negotiation process on Security Council reform. We trust that this session will help member states better understand the various reform proposals and foster the political will necessary for meaningful progress. The Common African position on the Security Council's working methods has been consistently restated and is well known within this process and the Assembly. Our position on working methods of the Security Council is reflected in paragraph 5 of our letter dated 23 December 2009 addressed to the then-chair of the IGN, contained in July 2015 document and its annex, also known as the Framework Document. Africa's position on the working methods of the Security Council calls for a council that is accessible, accountable, democratic, representative, and more effective, particularly in an expanded format to better address contemporary challenges. In this regard, we acknowledge the ongoing efforts to enhance the working methods of the Security Council. Especially the increase in the number of public meetings, briefings, open debates, and consultations between the presidents of the General Assembly and the Security Council. We also recognize the valuable initiative led by the delegation of Algeria within the Security Council concerning access to documentation, particularly as reflected in the new Note 507, which ensures that elected members of the Council have the same level of access to documentation submitted to or originated by the Security Council or its subsidiary bodies throughout their term of membership. Building on these efforts, Africa believes that further actions are required to improve the working methods of the Security Council in the following areas. First, the Security Council must uphold the primacy of the UN Charter in its functions and powers. To this end, it should refrain from engaging in or initiating formal or informal discussions regarding the situation in any member state on issues that do not constitute a threat to international peace and security, in accordance with the provisions of Article 24 of the Charter. Second, the Security Council should strengthen its relationship with troop-contributing countries and police-contributing countries, as well as the UN Secretariat, including through more sustained, regular, and timely interactions. Meetings with TCCs should not be limited to the drafting of mandates, but should also include discussions on the implementation phase, particularly when there is a rapid deterioration of the situation on the ground. The Security Council Working Group on Peacekeeping Operations should engage TCCs more frequently and intensively in its deliberations, particularly in the early stages of mission planning and throughout the mission's implementation. Third, the Security Council should establish its subsidiary organs in full accordance with the letter and spirit of the UN Charter. These organs must function in a manner that ensures the timely and adequate dissemination of information about their activities to the broader UN membership. Furthermore, The Security Council should avoid being used to pursue national political agendas. It must prioritize impartiality and non-selectivity in its work, adhering strictly to the powers and functions granted to it by the member states under the UN Charter. The Security Council must also refrain from using Chapter 7 of the Charter as a blanket approach to addressing issues that do not necessarily pose a threat to international peace and security. Instead, it should exhaust the provisions of Chapters 6 and 8 where appropriate, reserving Chapter 6 as a measure of last resort. Additionally, the Security Council should refrain from using sanctions against any state as a tool to achieve the political objectives of one or a few states rather than serving the broader interests of the international community. Distinguished co-chairs, let me reiterate that the common African position, as espoused in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Serté Declaration, stresses that any reform of the United Nations system should be comprehensive, encompassing all its components, including the need to enhance the Security Council's working methods. It is important to note that the 5 clusters outlined in Decision 62/ 557 cannot be discussed in isolation from the broader principles set out in paragraphs 152 to 154 of the World Summit Outcome Document of 2005. These principles—equity, geographical representation, transparency, efficiency, legitimacy, and accountability—are foundational to any reform process. Moreover, the linkages between the clusters cannot be overlooked. This means that none of the 5 clusters can be negotiated independently of the others. Expansion in both the permanent and non-permanent categories is closely connected to issues of size and the veto. An expanded Security Council will also require equitable geographical representation, underscoring the need for comprehensive reform of the Council. In conclusion, we reaffirm our commitment to Decision 62/557 and call for a comprehensive reform of the Security Council, one that reflects the interlinkages of the 5 clusters. We also acknowledge the important consensus in this regard to also prioritize Africa and treat Africa as a special case in the reform process in the Pact for the Future. Moving forward, we will continue consultations with all groups that have demonstrated strong support for the common African position and look forward to transforming empathy for our position into tangible support in line with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Cotonou Declaration. In the spirit of an inclusive reform outcome, we will also continue to engage with member states and interest groups holding different views on the reform process. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Sierra Leone, and I give the floor to Mamlakat al-Bahrain.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Arab Group. I would like to begin by expressing my sincere appreciation for your effort in conducting the work of the intergovernmental negotiations during the current session. We would also like to thank His Excellency Ambassador Alexander Marczyk, the permanent representative of the Republic of— the former permanent representative of the Republic of Austria to the United Nations, for his valuable efforts as co-chair of the IGN. Mr. Chair, the question of the working methods of the Security Council enjoys a convergence of positions and views on many of its elements. The Arab Group expresses its appreciation for the steps taken by the co-chairs during the last session to advance the discussion on the working methods of the current and future expanded council. This is especially pertinent to the Pact of the Future, which calls for the continued improvement and democratization of the working methods of the Council. The Pact also called for strengthening the Council's relationship with the General Assembly in accordance with the respective functions, authorities, powers, prerogatives, as set in the Charter. This is based on the understanding that this should not be an alternative to the reform of the Security Council. In light of the ongoing efforts of the Security Council to review and improve its working methods, the Arab Group emphasizes the importance of continuing to work to improve the Council's working methods and make it more transparent and inclusive. The Security Council is required to fulfill 2 important pillars. The first is to adopt decisions that ensure swift and effective action to maintain international peace and security. The second pillar is to obtain the support of the general membership to ensure the effective implementation of Security Council resolutions. Thus, enhancing the transparency of the working methods of the Security Council and ensuring the participation of the general membership in decision-making is critical to the performance of the Council. In this regard, consideration should be given to agreeing on permanent rules of procedures for the Security Council instead of the provisional ones that have been in place for decades. We should provide a real opportunity for non-members of the Security Council to contribute to the debate in the Council. We must minimize the holding of closed meetings and informal consultations to a minimum. The latter should be the exception rather than the rule, in accordance with the rules of procedures. There should also be consultations with and participation of countries concerned on items under discussion in the Security Council. In the same context, the Arab Group attaches importance to the subsidiary organs of the Security Council and its committees. We call for the provision of comprehensive information on their activities to the members of the United Nations. Particularly the states concerned in the case of sanctions committees. We emphasize the need for the Security Council to strictly adhere to the scope and mandate of its resolutions on the work of subsidiary committees. The Arab Group would also like to stress the importance of the participation of the Peacebuilding Commission and its country-specific configurations. We should take into account their views during Security Council discussions. on the issues on the agenda of the Security Council and that of the Peacebuilding Commission. In light of the clear relationship between the General Assembly and the Security Council pursuant to the relevant articles and provisions of the UN Charter, the Arab Group believes that it is important for the Security Council to share and inform the General Assembly of the issues before it. This would increase transparency between the General Assembly and the Security Council. It would also support complementarity between the 2 organs, enhance the exchange of views, and enable the GA to fulfill its role when discussing different issues. In conclusion, I would like to reiterate that the 5 reform clusters are interrelated and indivisible. The intergovernmental negotiations are the only forum that would allow us to reach an agreement on the issue of the Security Council expansion and reform pursuant to GA Resolution 557, which calls for a solution that enjoys the widest possible political acceptance. The Arab Group encourages the continuation of discussions in a positive atmosphere with a view to converging views and finding common ground to achieve substantive and radical reform of the Security Council. For this is the body entrusted with the maintenance of international peace and security pursuant to the Charter of the United Nations. This would allow the Council to become more capable and more effective in addressing and overcoming relevant challenges in a more representative, transparent, impartial, and credible framework. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
I would like to thank His Excellency the Representative of the Kingdom of Bahrain.

Thank you very much, Co-Chair. Excellencies, dear colleagues, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the Benelux countries— Belgium, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and my own country, Luxembourg— for today's meeting of the IGN. Co-Chair, you have asked us to focus on working methods. The topic of working methods is vast. And constantly evolving. If we look back at Decision 62557 of 15 September 2008, the foundational decision by which the General Assembly decided to commence intergovernmental negotiations, we see that the 5 key issues on which the IGN are based do not include working methods as a standalone issue. Rather, Decision 62557 mentions as the 4th key issue the following, I quote, size of an enlarged Security Council and working methods of the Council, unquote. In our view, this clearly signifies that while the working methods of the Security Council can be continuously improved, without structural reform of the Council, and many colleagues who have spoken before me have mentioned some examples in that regard, the IGN on Security Council reform should focus on the adaptation of the Council's working methods that are needed to accommodate an expanded membership of the Council. Such an understanding should allow us to focus our discussion in the IGN and we should not duplicate discussions that are held elsewhere on the continuous improvement of the Council's working methods and the implementation of Note 507 by the President of the Security Council, the most recent edition of which was adopted in December last year. Co-Chair, the most recent Co-Chairs' Elements Paper that you have circulated on 29 April 2024 shows that there is a very high degree of convergence when it comes to adapting the Council's working methods to the size of an enlarged Council. And building on these commonalities, we can make concrete progress toward a more representative and effective Security Council. The Benelux countries in particular support the need to adjust the required number of affirmative votes required for decisions by the Security Council in line with the current practice or ratio. We also support the idea that the Security Council, in light of the increase in its membership, should be invited to consider measures to ensure the full and equitable participation of all members of the Security Council in its work with a special emphasis on encouraging greater participation and responsibilities of non-permanent members, elected members, including the opportunity to serve as penholders and to hold the presidency of the enlarged Security Council at least once during their tenure. Co-chair, colleagues, by adopting the Pact for the Future, we agreed on all the guiding principles. Of Security Council reform, including on the principle that the total number of members of an enlarged Security Council should ensure a balance between its representativeness and effectiveness— that is Action 39E of the Pact— and we agreed on the principle that the working methods should ensure the inclusive, transparent, efficient, effective, democratic, and accountable functioning of an enlarged Council, that is Action 39F of the Pact. Based on the Pact for the Future and the clear convergences identified in the co-chairs' elements paper, the Benelux countries believe that the next logical step is to move towards text-based negotiations, ensuring that our discussions don't go around in circles but rather translate into concrete outcomes. This year we will mark the 80th anniversary of the founding of the United Nations at a time when multilateralism is increasingly being challenged. We should seize this opportunity to make progress in the IGN on Security Council reform. We should indeed move from general discussions of the 5 key issues identified in Decision 62557 which have been thoroughly debated over the last 16 years, to detailed discussions on specific models for Council reform. And as we have agreed in the Pact for the Future, we should develop a consolidated model that will lead us to a reformed Security Council, a Council that is more representative, inclusive, transparent, efficient, effective, democratic and accountable to the wider membership. Thank you very much, Co-Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Luxembourg. I give the floor to Brazil.

Thank you, dear Co-Chair. As others, I join— I join others in thanking you and the former PR of Austria for the dedication, your commitment to progress and movement forward in this discussion. I deliver this statement on behalf of the G4, that is Germany, India, Japan, and my own country, Brazil. Today's meeting on the working methods of a reformed Security Council is yet another one in a long series of cluster-based discussions. On the issue at hand, we fully acknowledge that improvements to the Council's working methods can help enhance its efficiency, transparency, and inclusivity. In this spirit, we commend Japan's leadership in revising Note 507 during its IWG chairpersonship, a practical step forward in modernizing the Council's procedures. Enhanced transparency, equitable penholdership, and closer cooperation with the GA and the PBC are important and beneficial and should be fully implemented. Distinguished Co-Chair, however, we must be clear: any procedural adjustments, however meaningful they are in their own right, are not a substitute for structural reform, as other delegations have mentioned. The legitimacy and effectiveness of the Security Council depend fundamentally on comprehensive reform, particularly the expansion in its permanent and non-permanent membership, that reflects the realities of today's world. I emphasize the importance of having a comprehensive outlook in this regard, as a piecemeal approach is bound to fail. The time for inconsequential IGN debates that generate little concrete results— if there was ever such time— has long passed. If Member States are serious about making the Council accountable and credible, legitimate and effective, we must all unequivocally and immediately support text-based negotiations in a time-bound manner, wherein actionable steps are linked to defined timelines. This is the only realistic path for overcoming our deep differences. Once again, our focus must shift from general discussions of the 5 clusters, which are clearly exhausted, to examining specific models presented during this IGN cycle and developing a consolidated model that can facilitate genuine reform. To this end, We call on all delegations willing to do so to present concrete reform models to their earliest convenience, as the preparation of the consolidated model must strike the right balance between inclusiveness and movement forward. Anything less only further undermines the IGN process. I thank you, Co-Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil. And I give the floor to Iceland.

Excellencies, co-chairs, I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the Nordic countries— Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and my own country, Iceland. Co-chairs, in the Pact for the Future adopted by the General Assembly last September, It was agreed to strengthen the framework of the intergovernmental negotiations on Security Council reform as a matter of priority and without delay. Not only does the Pact for the Future deliver a clear statement on the need to reform the Security Council, it also notes specific objectives to that end when discussing the importance of working methods, noting in Action 39F that the working methods should ensure the inclusive, transparent, efficient, effective, democratic, and accountable functioning of an enlarged Council. This provides us with specific agreed language and guidance, and it should be the basis of any discussion on working methods going forward. It should be our aim to consolidate and build on this language, as we are entrusted to ensure that an enlarged Security Council is able to deliver on its mandate and become fit for purpose. Before diving further into the topic, we wish to underline the distinction between working methods reform required to accommodate an expanded Council and those working methods issues we are already encountering with the Council in its current configuration. While both issues should be addressed as a matter of urgency, The latter should not await a comprehensive reform of the Council through the IGN process. Co-chairs, with reference to the working methods, the Security Council is expected to firstly make decisions that will ensure prompt and effective action to maintain international peace and security, and secondly gain the support of the wider United Nations membership for such Security Council decisions to be carried out. Enhancing the transparency, efficiency, and inclusiveness of the working methods of the Security Council in order to meet these expectations is crucial to the effective functioning of the Council. In this regard, the Nordic countries note that strengthened accountability, efficiency, and inclusiveness starts with transparency. Transparency may be reinforced through through increased dialogue with and involvement of non-Council members and bodies, in particular affected member states and civil society. Moreover, transparency may also be strengthened with added emphasis on increasing resources to open meetings and agreeing on a wider array of press elements. At the same time, the Nordic countries recognize that private discussions are paramount to FRAG diplomatic talks and the building of trust and cooperation among different members of the Security Council. But such discussions must be coupled with, as just mentioned, once common elements of transparency, like the routine issue of press elements from closed consultations. The Nordics note that the Pact for the Future calls for the working methods to ensure democratic functions, a core issue at the heart of the Security Council reform. In this context, the Nordics reiterate our support for a balanced expansion of the Security Council to ensure increased representation. We further support consideration on how to ensure the consistent application of Article 27 of the Charter. We also call on the IGN process and the Council to ensure that working methods in a future Council are guided by the fundamental principles of democracy, and that democratic values are generally strengthened. We must ensure that the working methods are updated so that an expansion of the Council does not negatively impact the full participation of all Security Council members in its work, in particular the elected members. We note that depending on the ultimate size of an enlarged Council, there may be need to revise the existing rotation rule of the Council presidency. In order to ensure that all elected members have the opportunity to hold the presidency at least during at least once during their tenure. Also, further work is needed in order to strengthen the role of elected members, in particular so that the elected members play a full role in all aspects of the council's work and can better fulfill the role as a member of the council and representatives of the general membership. Of the United Nations. This can be further strengthened through a fairer burden sharing amongst the P5s and elected members. The informal penholder system should be adapted and pens shared across the Council, especially where there is expertise or where an elected member is chairing the relevant subsidiary body. The perspectives of the relevant regions should be taken into account across the work of the Council. With African peace and security continuing to take up much of the Security Council's agenda, it is clear that more African voices are needed and African member states should have a more profound influence over its work. We would like to see more opportunities for the African members of the Council for penholdership or co-penholdership. Co-chairs, the general improvement of the working methods of the Council is an ongoing process. and a collective endeavour. The Nordic countries commend the progress made so far, and we look forward to the next steps. Reform is urgent and cannot wait. Finally, Co-Chairs, the Nordic countries reiterate our support for all your persistent work efforts towards Security Council reform. We shall continuously strive to meet the commitments and momentum achieved with the Pact. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Iceland.

And I give the floor to the Republic of Egypt.

Thank you, Mr. Chair.

I'm going to start by aligning with the statements delivered by Sierra Leone on behalf of the African Group and by Bahrain on behalf of the Arab Group.

Thank you.

The working methods of the Security Council is a fundamental aspect of the Council reform. As outlined in Resolution 62557, improved and enhanced working methods shall be a component of the final comprehensive reform package. Despite this pillar often, often being overlooked in favor of the more big-ticket items such as the veto or categories of membership, enhanced and strengthened working methods remain a crucial aspect of the work of a reformed Security Council. One without which the Council could never be able to perform its functions soundly. In the Pact of the Future, Member States agreed a number of important provisions relating to improving the Council's working methods. In Action 41, we commit to actively reinforce the ongoing efforts of the Security Council to review and enhance its working methods, including inter alia penholding and co-penholding arrangements, and to strengthen the cooperation and communication between the Security Council Security Council and the General Assembly and its subsidiary bodies. These provisions reaffirm the importance member states attach to enhancing the Council's working methods, and indeed some improvements have been introduced in recent years. Yet if we are to ensure an inclusive, transparent, efficient, effective, democratic, and accountable functioning of an enlarged Council as per Action 39 of the Pact, more effort needs to be done. A few areas come to mind. First, the Council needs to enhance its engagement with the wider membership while avoiding selectivity, double standards, and politicization in the exercising of its mandate. This necessitates a further increase in the number of open debates, public briefings, and interactive dialogues, in addition to giving countries under consideration at the Council and troops-contributing countries a say in the processes of relevance to them. Second, democratization of decision-making inside the Council. One aspect of decision-making in dire need of such reform, for example, is penholdership, and while huge improvements have taken place, certain members of the Council still remain exclusive penholders for certain issues. It should never be forgotten that penholdership is merely a drafting task taken up by Council members and that it does not by any means entail political dominance over the matter under consideration. Third, meetings of the subsidiary bodies of the Council should include on a case-by-case basis non-Council members showing interest and possessing the relevant expertise. Member states, particularly those affected by sanctions, should at their request be allowed to participate in the meetings of the relevant sanctions committee. These are just a few ideas for consideration, and I trust that several other ideas will be have been and will be discussed. Discussed today and in the following meetings, and we remain confident that without a reform of the working methods, the reform of the Security Council will still be incomplete. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Egypt, and I give the floor to Germany.

Thank you very much, Co-Chair. At the outset, I would like to underline that Germany aligns itself fully with the statement that has been delivered by Brazil on behalf of the Group of Four. But I would like to take the opportunity to make 2 additional points in my national capacity. The first is on a more general reflection on working methods. I think in all the statements that we heard today, transparency, efficiency, accountability were raised. For us, all 3— transparency, efficiency, and accountability— are not just matters of presentation when it comes to the work of the Security Council. For us, all 3 are fundamental to the effectiveness and ultimately to the legitimacy of the Security Council. In the past year, we had a very lengthy but ultimately quite productive discussion on this matter during the negotiations of the Pact for the Future, and I think it has been raised by almost all delegations this morning at least I remember it being quoted by Bahrain, Sierra Leone, Luxembourg, Iceland, Egypt, that we should really follow up on the conclusions of the Pact when it comes to the Security Council. For instance, the Pact for the Future clearly emphasizes the importance of strengthening the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly and its subsidiary bodies. As the current Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, Germany is strongly committed to realizing the full potential of this Commission and to fostering a more effective division of labor and greater synergies between the Peacebuilding Commission and the Security Council. We are convinced that by working together we can ensure that both the Peacebuilding Commission plays a more prominent role in peacebuilding efforts and at the same time the Security Council is better equipped and better informed. Mr. Chair, my second remark is on the use of the veto. Germany supports all efforts and initiatives to limit the use of the veto, particularly in cases where the veto is used to block Council action aimed at the prevention and punishment of genocide, mass atrocities, and war crimes, and we call on other member states to join these initiatives. We would also like to remind delegations that the G4 model promotes the idea of new permanent members who have the power to veto but refrain from using it for an initial period of time. We believe that this is a viable reform idea worthy of consideration. Mr. Chair, in conclusion, I would just like to reiterate that we are committed to engaging in constructive dialogue with other IGN members on these issues. With the goal of finding a path forward that promotes transparency, efficiency, and accountability within the Security Council.
I thank you very much. I thank the distinguished representative of Germany, and I give the floor to India.

Shukran jazil, and see you at the—

Thank you very much, Mr.

Chair. I wish to convey our appreciation for the dynamism demonstrated by the Chair in imparting new momentum. I align myself with the statements delivered by Saint Vincent and the Grenadines on behalf of L69 and Brazil on behalf of G4. The previous speakers have already emphasized the pressing need for undertaking reforms of the Security Council on priority. The demand in this chamber for reforms is loud and clear. This call gains greater significance at a time when the world is expressing apprehensions at the ability of the United Nations to deliver to meaningfully intervene on issues of key importance to humanity in different parts of the globe, particularly in the realm of peace and security, which remains the core mandate of the Council. It is beyond doubt that the Security Council represents a different period of time. The core architecture, which has remained unchanged for 8 decades, is not in synchrony with today's global realities. To realize its functional mandate to match the expectations of the people, our citizens, and to maintain contemporary relevance, the Council needs to be made fit for purpose. Though an overwhelming number of member states acknowledge that reforms are indeed an imperative, there has been practically no progress along this direction. We have had numerous discussions and debates. We speak passionately, but we continue to be where we are. Co-chairs and colleagues, we cannot be losing any more time in exchanging ideas and engaging in discussions alone. It's time for member states to act. It's time to move forward. It's time to show results. In this backdrop, I'd like to make following specific points with regard to working methods. First, the Council needs to engage with the wider membership of the United Nations. A meaningful way to achieve this would be through a discussion on the report of the Security Council in the General Assembly. This report should not be merely a compilation of facts. It should be analytical in nature, offering an opportunity for the member states to effectively appraise the functioning of the Council. Second, there needs to be more transparency in the working of the subsidiary bodies of the Council. Let me give a specific example. While decisions on listing are made public, details pertaining to rejection or putting on technical hold of listing requests are the exclusive preserve of a select few. This is indeed a disguised veto. Third, implementation of peacekeeping mandate should duly factor in the concerns of troop and police contributing countries. For India, as the largest cumulative troop contributor, this remains a key issue. Fourth, obsolete and irrelevant items with no relevance in today's world have no basis to remain on the agenda of the Security Council merely for political purposes. Fifth, reforms pertaining to one cluster cannot be considered in isolation. A piecemeal approach is bound to fail. Therefore, the question of Council reforms needs to be dealt with in its entirety, in a holistic manner. In closing, I'd like to reiterate that the world does not have the luxury to hide behind the smokescreen of intergovernmental negotiations, a process which has no timeframe and no text to achieve real reforms. The pathway to reform starts with a text and attaching fixed timelines to achieving concrete outcomes. May I add that the reform of the working methods of the intergovernmental negotiation process itself is thus a very good starting point. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of India. I give the floor to Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. Japan fully aligns with Brazil's statement on behalf of the G4. I will make additional remarks in my national capacity. As the international community faces numerous challenges and the role expected of the Security Council increases, it has become imperative to further enhance the effective functioning of the Council, which shoulders the primary responsibility of maintaining international peace and security. Enhancing the transparency efficiency, and inclusiveness of the working method is in particular a reform that can be achieved without amending the UN Charter. It is therefore crucial to continuously improve the working methods. It was in 2006 that Japan, as a chair of Informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions, IWG, reviewed the practices and agreements on the working methods of the Security Council, which had been recorded in more than 100 presidential notes since the establishment of the IWG in 1993. Japan systematically compiled the presidential notes, which are effective as of 2006, and in July of that year, the first Note 507 was adopted as a compilation of the working methods of the Security Council at that time. Since then, Japan has chaired the IWG every time it has served as an elected member of the Security Council and led the successful efforts to adopt the updated Note 507 in 2010 and again in 2017. Last year, Japan chaired the IWG again, and through an open debate in March and intensive discussions in the IWG, The updated Note 507 was finally adopted on December 13th last year. I am pleased that Japan's initiative to compile the adopted presidential notes and relevant documents into one handbook is now well known as Green Book, as the COVID page of that latest one is green. Following the completion of its most recent 2-year Security Council term, Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Japan remains committed to improving the Council's working methods, aiming for greater transparency and efficiency. To facilitate the implementation of the adopted rules and provisions, Japan is in the process of preparing the new printed edition of the Handbook, which is planned to distribute at an event scheduled next month. Mr. Chair, While we are at the center of efforts to improving working methods, we must point out that this is only an internal measure, and the core of Security Council reform is the expansion of both permanent and non-permanent categories in the Security Council. It is regrettable that the Pact for the Future adopted last year did not take into account the objective fact the majority of the member states supports the expansion of both permanent and non-permanent categories. In developing a consolidated model in the IGN, it is crucial to stipulate the expansion of both permanent and non-permanent categories, especially to redress the historical injustice against Africa. As set out in the Pact for the Future, Security Council reform is urgently needed. For this very reason, it is imperative to initiate text-based negotiations as soon as possible. Capitalizing on the 80th anniversary of the UN Foundation this year, Japan reiterates its commitment to make a constructive contribution to the ongoing discussions in the IGN, ensuring the UN aligns with the contemporary global landscape. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan, and I give the floor to France.

Mr. Co-chair, first of all, I would like to thank you and the Austrian co-chair for organizing this 3rd debate. Security Council reform is expected by the vast majority of this assembly. We reaffirmed this in the Pact for the Future. We are celebrating the 80th anniversary of the Charter. We must go from words to action. For France, the objectives of this reform are clear. The Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Jean-Noël Barrault, said this clearly before the General Assembly and then in Addis Ababa and before the members of the G20. They are improving the representativeness of the Security Council, in particular for the sake of— to the benefit of Africa. Preserving its legitimacy as the cornerstone in our collective security architecture, and strengthening its efficiency and effectiveness. The path to achieving this is known by everyone. It is provided for in the United Nations Charter and has been used several times, including to reform the Security Council in 1963. It involves the adoption of a resolution in the General Assembly with the support of at least 2/3 of member states. France calls for the immediate launching of text-based negotiations and, like the majority of delegations, calls for an expansion in the 2 categories of membership. France supports the creation of 2 permanent seats for African states and the creation of permanent seats for the Group of 4— Germany, India, Japan, and Brazil. This is not new, and I'm repeating it today. Co-chairs, regarding the Security Council's working methods, the aim is to find the proper balance between public diplomacy and work behind closed doors to make sure that the Council can play its role, and that role is the maintenance of international peace and security. Public meetings are useful because they allow for greater openness and transparency, They also make sure that the voice of civil society can be heard. Discussions behind closed doors allow compromises to be reached among all of the members of the Council on a text that is to be adopted. That allows for a broad and enlightened expression on the part of the Council. Improving the Council's working methods means being able to conduct substantive work in a spirit of respect for multilateralism. In the— if that were not to happen, the Council would find itself pronouncing itself on an insufficient approximative text that would be put to a vote without taking into account the views of the main stakeholders. But let us be clear-headed. Improving the working methods is necessary, but it's not enough. It doesn't replace the spirit of responsibility that is essential in order to find solutions to crises. It doesn't replace the need for having the Charter, the sovereign equality of states, and respect for the territorial integrity of states as our compass. When on the 24th of February 2025 in the Security Council, 6 member states refused to support references to the Charter, our shared Charter, and to its principles, including sovereignty and territorial integrity, it was not just working methods that were at issue. When Russia used its veto twice on amendments covering those messages and those essential principles, it was not just working methods that were at issue. When on the same day, 10 members of the Security Council voted for a resolution that skipped over respect for the Charter and its principles, even though the United Nations General Assembly had affirmed the importance of the Charter and its principles twice a few hours beforehand, it was not just working methods that were at issue. What is at issue is respect for international law and the primacy of law over force and the work of all of the organs of the United Nations. Mr. Co-chairs, on the 24th of February, 2025, France did not use its veto against an unjust resolution because we advocate for a responsible use of the veto. Since 2015, we have done that with Mexico and the support of 106 United Nations member states. This initiative of limiting the use of the veto in the case of— to the case of mass atrocities, that is to say genocide, crimes against humanity, and large-scale war crimes, aims to give the Security Council the tools it needs to act in those situations And I call upon all member states that believe in peace through law to join us in that. This initiative doesn't require an amendment of the Charter, and it does not create inequalities with new permanent members. And I recall that France considers that candidates for those seats can legitimately ask for the same prerogatives as the current permanent members, including the right of veto. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of France. France, and I give the floor to the Russian Federation.

Distinguished co-chairs, we welcome the continued consideration of the thematic clusters on UN Security Council reform in the context of the intergovernmental negotiations. We closely studied the renewed Security Council model that was circulated by CARICOM And we hope to be able to discuss it in detail during one of the upcoming meetings of the intergovernmental negotiations. Improving the Council's working methods is an important aspect of ensuring the effectiveness of the organ that bears primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. When executing its mandate, the Security Council should be in lockstep with the times and be able to take well-thought-through, timely, and sustainable decisions. In recent years, this organ has been holding more open meetings, regularly organizing informal ARIA formula meetings of its members, and listening to the positions of states that are not members of the Council. A leading role in the process of updating the Security Council working methods continues to be played by the Council itself, which within its Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural questions holds a regular review of existing practice. The most recent significant result from this was the latest update of Note 507 in December last year. In particular, the document reflects the procedure for Security Council members accessing internal documentation. The section on informal penholdership has been expanded, and Russia consistently calls for strict compliance with all of the provisions in Note 507 in full. Any further changes on this track need to be geared towards truly improving the effectiveness and efficiency of the Council in fulfilling its main tasks. The use of poorly thought-out initiatives that don't take into account the specifics of the Council's work is counterproductive. For example, we categorically disagree with the proposal to do away with closed consultations. As practice has shown, it is behind closed doors that the Council can have an open dialogue and reach the necessary compromise on the most complex issues on its agenda. Open meetings, on the other hand, often are geared towards a domestic audience and boil down to repeating well-known positions in front of the cameras, which does nothing to bring positions closer together. They're not— they don't take account of the interests of other states, and they're not always able to find a balanced assessment given their geopolitical ambitions and regional specificities. The abuse of their informal status— in abusing their informal status, the penholders often negotiate resolutions of the Security Council under artificial time pressure that does not allow for a comprehensive expert study of the documents. Instead of discussions of the text in good faith, In those circumstances, they focus on putting pressure on the non-permanent members of the council that do not agree with them, and quite simply, they twist their arms. As a result, we often have poorly thought-out documents that do not take into account the key concerns of Security Council members, which give unclear instructions to the Secretariat, and which are sometimes unrealistic in terms of their goals and targets. This approach. Does nothing to support the effective settlement of conflicts. Russia consistently has advocated for and continues to advocate for expanding the number of penholders, primarily from among the non-permanent members. In particular, we pay attention to the opinions of African states in doing so. We are convinced that looking again at the issue of penholdership will help improve the effectiveness of the Security Council's work. In sum, improving the working methods must be continued by the Council on a regular basis according to the established procedure and on the basis of a rational study of its experience on an annual basis. A certain contribution to this could be made by the intergovernmental negotiations on Security Council reform. At the same time, we call upon colleagues to focus as a priority on the fundamental parts of reform, first and foremost on increasing— improving the representation on the Security Council of the countries of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, while ensuring that it also remains compact. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation, and I give the floor to Mexico.

Co-facilitators, Mexico would like to align with the statement delivered by Italy on behalf of the Uniting for Consensus Group. Allow me to deliver A few additional comments in my national capacity. The discussion of the working methods of a reformed Security Council is not just a matter of form but of substance. That's because any proposal to expand its membership force includes a thorough analysis of its functioning. Focusing merely on increasing the number of members without having an in-depth look at how the working methods of a reformed council would work would lead to inefficiencies which could curtail the ability of the council to respond in a timely and effective way to threats to international peace and security. Because of this, we once again appeal to the various negotiating groups and delegations which have presented reform models or those which which are about to present them so that their analyses also take an in-depth look at how their proposals fully chime with the 5 clusters of Decision 62/557. The foregoing doesn't just allow us to understand the scope of their proposals but also to assess their effectiveness. Proposed reforms which merely focus on 1 or 2 clusters are not enough. Mexico believes that all members, especially elected members, must participate on an equal footing and have the guarantee— possibility of leading the subsidiary bodies of the Security Council, as well as acting as penholders or co-penholders for resolutions and the right to take up the presidency of that body throughout their mandate. To enhance the transparency of the subsidiary bodies, Mexico believes there's a need to improve the quality, frequency, and availability of their official and unofficial reports, as well as their meeting records. That would allow states who are not part of the Council to be better informed and more effectively participate in the debates and decisions related to the work of that body. Turning now to the chairship of subsidiary bodies, Mexico is of the view that in a reformed council it should be made clear that the 5 permanent members should not have veto power over which elected member chairs a subsidiary body. Regrettably, we have seen this practice as a form of overstepping of the powers of the 5 permanent members. This situation is tangible right now with the delay probably never before seen in the election of the chairs of the subsidiary bodies for 2025. Along similar lines, council reform should consider that the Security Council should not be the only vote which counts in the election of the Secretary-General. The General Assembly should have greater importance in that decision. In terms of draft decisions, presidents' declarations, press releases, elements of the press and presidential notes, all of these should be made available to non-member states in a way which is timely and observes the principle of multilingualism which governs our organization. Interrelatedness of working reform working methods and the veto. Mexico calls upon further states to join the Franco-Mexican proposal. We believe that this initiative could be duly codified within the context of a reformed council. Mexico, in its reform model, presented a list of seven initial measures which could be complemented and. Strengthened to ensure that the working methods of a reformed Security Council correct other imbalances which are not merely resolved with the addition of new seats. Uniting for Consensus also presented a similar list. These measures have been the outcome of discussions we held in the context of the IGN and our national experience as a country which served as an elected member in recent times. To conclude, we would reiterate that to achieve a reform which enables us to have a more democratic, transparent, representative, effective council which has better accountability, we need to substantially— substantively consider the improvement of the working methods as they stand today. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico and I give the floor to Pakistan.

Thank you. Thank you, Co-Chair. I would like to start by acknowledging the splendid work that was done by Ambassador Maschek and yourself over the past 2 years. We will miss Ambassador Maschek. But we are very glad to see you are holding the fort and guiding our process. Co-chair, everyone is agreed that Security Council reform is necessary and that it should be achieved as soon as possible. But I'd like to also note that the Pact of the Future called for comprehensive measures to strengthen the entire United Nations system. The actions listed in the Pact called for strengthening the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, and the peacebuilding Commission as well, and I think that we should all focus on moving on all fronts as far as the reform of the United Nations bodies is concerned. We attach importance to. The process that we are following. We do not believe that we are at the present moment in a stage where we can launch text-based negotiations or set some sort of an artificial deadline for the conclusion of our discussions. One of my colleagues has mentioned the need to reflect new realities, but the realities that we reflect in a Council expansion of permanent members would again freeze the Council at a particular time, as it is frozen in the 1945 framework, Any expansion of permanent members would freeze the Council at that moment. It is only through the process of elections that the new realities that constantly change can be reflected in the composition of the Security Council. Not by adding new permanent members. Our discussions for the Pact of the Future and the in the IGN last year revealed where the convergences are and where the divergences are. There is convergence on priority for Africa. There is convergence on. Expanding the membership of developing countries. There is a convergence on the need for representation of regional and cross-regional groups. And these are convergences that we can build on and that have been confirmed in the models for Security Council reform that have been presented. But these discussions and the presentation of models has also revealed the divergences, and these are considerable divergences on the size of the Council, on the issue of the categories of membership, on regional representation, on the veto, and on even on working methods where there is a large convergence, yet there are still areas Of divergence, and these have been reflected in our discussions here today. The discussion on working methods, co-chair, is not marginal to the reform of the Security Council. As was famously said, process is substance. And the working methods of the Council impact on its outcomes and its processes. My delegation has proposed a number of steps that could be taken to ensure improvement in the working methods of the Council. These have not all been reflected in Note 507, Although there have been some improvements. We need several things. We need first of all transparency, and transparency requires open meetings, the application of Rule 48 of the Provisional Rules of Procedure of the Security Council, more interactive open meetings, not set-piece statements that are made without any thought to interaction and action by the Council. There is most importantly the need for democracy, and that democracy can be inducted through the role of elected members, not permanent members. We need to have a larger role for the elected members And to break the oligopoly of the P5 in the Security Council. And this is manifest in at least 4 areas. Firstly, the penhold issue. There is an imbalance in the holding of pens between the P5 and the E10, and there is also an imbalance in the holding of pens between and among the P5, where some members hold a majority of the pens, and there is one permanent member who holds no pen and has been prevented from exercising pen holdership on one issue quite recently. So I think there is a need to review the whole process and I believe that the Security Council's Working Group will look into this and we hope this group will contribute and support this reform of the penholdership. Secondly, the issue of selection of chairs of subsidiary bodies. Again, these are arbitrarily vetoed in certain cases, arbitrarily, with no reason and no transparency. There must be a greater transparent process for selection or rejection of a chair for various groups. Certain groups cannot monopolize areas that are critical. Thirdly, the issue of documentation. Our Algerian friends have talked about the access, equal access to documentation, and they had to fight for it. It was not automatic. And fourthly, there is the issue of The revision of the periodicity of meetings of the subsidiary bodies. If you see the schedule, there are very few meetings. The subsidiary bodies exist, but they meet very infrequently, and there are good reasons for that. And we have to look into that. Thirdly, there is the issue of representation. There has to be a greater role for regional bodies and for cross-regional groups to be represented in all the interactive discussions Fourthly, the issue of accountability. We have sanctions regimes which are applied and adopted almost automatically when an issue comes before the Council. It's as if you have a hammer and you see everything as a nail. So that sanctions regimes are applied, and these are often counterproductive. When you apply sanctions regime on a country that is in internal conflict or in a crisis, it impacts on the population of that country and is counterproductive. And therefore, we have called— Pakistan has called for a review of the sanctions regimes of the Security Council. And we believe that the whole issue of how Chapter 7 resolutions are adopted needs to be reconsidered. Quite often, Chapter 7 resolutions are presented by P5 members or some P5 members without consultations with the E10 and imposed within 24, 48, 72 hours as such. And I think this is This is not an accountable process and it needs to be reviewed. There is also the issue of detailed reporting, and I think my colleague from India mentioned it. We need more detailed reports from the Security Council to the General Assembly as to what has happened, what are the results of processes, not just a listing of issues. And lastly, the issue of the monitoring and implementation of Security Council resolutions. The Security Council has no mechanism by which it can monitor the implementation of resolutions. We need to find a mechanism, perhaps first and foremost a compendium of unimplemented resolutions of the Security Council. And here I would say there are no— old items do not die. The Security Council resolutions are not rescinded by non-implementation over time. Security Council resolutions under Article 25 are binding. Those have to be implemented, but we have no mechanism to review implementation. I think this is an important reform that we need in the Council. Co-chairs, we will work with you constructively and we hope that we will find even greater convergence on the issue of working methods. This will be an important component of the convergences on the 5 clusters. Once we have convergence on the 5 clusters, we would be willing to move to the next stage of the negotiations, but I'm afraid we are not there yet. The divergences are still too large and too difficult at the moment. Thank you, Co-Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative. Thank you, Representative of Pakistan. And I give the floor to Switzerland.

Mr. President.

Chairman, allow me first of all to thank Ambassador Marshek for his commitment and outstanding work in co-leading our work alongside you. I'd also like to thank you, sir. We welcome this thematic debate on working methods. Now, regardless of the composition of the Council, efficient and transparent working methods are essential, and we welcome the recognition of that need in the framework of the Pact for the Future. Switzerland, which has recently completed its mandate as an elected member, has been working for many years to improve these, notably as coordinator of the Accountability, Cohesion, and Transparency Group. Over the past 2 years, we have seen the importance of clear procedural rules and their consistent application, particularly in a context where substantive discussions are becoming ever more contentious. We commend the work of Albania in 2023 and Japan in 2024 as chairs of the Informal Working Group on Documentation and Procedural Matters. As well as the recent adoption of the update to Note 507 containing the most recent agreements on the Council's working methods. Despite this progress, we remain concerned by the erosion in the consistent application of these rules and the failure to respect the principles enshrined in the United Nations Charter. In particular, The obligation for parties to a dispute to refrain from voting as stipulated in Article 27 of the Charter has not been repeatedly— has been repeatedly disregarded, notably during last Monday's votes. Similarly, 5 months after the date specified in Note 507, no agreement has yet been reached on the distribution of the chairs of the Council subsidiary bodies. The legitimacy of the Council's decisions also depend on the way in which they are taken. Efficient and transparent working rules should— must be at the core of the functioning of the current Council and will be even more crucial in the context of an enlarged Council. In this context, Switzerland would like to highlight 3 priority areas that need to be strengthened. Increasing transparency. The Council's legitimacy also depends on the transparency of its work, which should be further improved and could involve better use of its means of communication. For instance, by institutionalizing the practice of the presidency making comments to the press following closed consultations, or by communicating the text prepared for the vote and their co-sponsors to all member states in real time. Like last year's visit to Colombia, which Switzerland co-led with the United Kingdom and Guyana, field missions are also a powerful instrument of engagement, communication, and transparency that the Council should use more often. Second, strengthening participation. During its Council presidencies in May 2023 and October 2024, Switzerland endeavored to increase the involvement of civil society representatives and to strengthen the participation of women in its deliberations. We must also ensure that a future Council is more representative, not only geographically, but also in the line— in line with the Women, Peace and Security and Youth, Peace and Security agendas. Third, better foresight. In October 2024, the Council adopted a presidential statement on the impact of scientific developments on international peace and security. As this document emphasizes, Switzerland believes that it is important to anticipate future developments, but also to strengthen interaction with scientific actors and make full use of their resorts in order to put the power of science at the service of peace and security. Chair, the Council must always strive to be effective in its work of maintaining international peace and security. While we favor A Council that better reflects today's world, we also advocate for a Council that is more capable of taking action. In the face of current and future challenges, the peoples of the world should expect nothing less. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Switzerland and I give the floor to Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Improving the Security Council's working method is central to our effort in making the Council more effective effective, efficient, transparent, inclusive, and accountable. It is key to ensure the Council is better fit for purpose in responding to the evolving security landscape. And not less importantly, improving the Council's working method is crucial to maintain the Council's credibility and legitimacy. Towards this direction, allow me to share 4 points. First, ensuring greater opportunities of non-Council members to engage with the Security Council. Regular consultation between the Council and wider member states on specific issues must be increased, such as with the TPCCs on the mandates of the UNPKO, as well as with relevant member states on sanctions. Among others, views from non-Council members on how to improve the annual report of the Security Council can be taken into consideration, in particular on how to make the report more analytical and reflects the trend in a year that enhances transparency and accountability, ultimately strengthening the effectiveness of the Council. Second, promoting more interactions between the Council with regional organizations and other subsidiary bodies, including the Peacebuilding Commission. Strengthening the collaboration will foster synergy and better understanding on real situation on the ground. It will lead to more concrete and effective responses. We also support continued interactions between the Informal Working Group on Documentation and Other Procedural Questions, or the IWG, with the IGN process. It is therefore important for the IGN to receive regular briefing from the IWG Chair to update the discussion in the Council. Third, ensuring greater equality between the E10 and the permanent members. The E10 must have equal opportunities as the penholders of issues based on the principles of openness, shared responsibility, and fair burden sharing among all Council members. Also, in the reformed Council, a mechanism should be arranged to ensure that each member of the Security Council serves as President of the Council at least once during their term. Lastly, a periodic review of the working method must be in place after the reform takes place, to identify further areas for improvement and incorporate feedbacks, and to ensure that the working methods remain adaptable for the Council to respond to continuously evolving challenges. Co-chairs, improving the working methods is part of the whole reform of the Security Council that we must undertake. A comprehensive reform process will only be achieved with our proactive approach and and strong political will. Therefore, let us demonstrate our utmost political commitment in making progress to reforming the Security Council that will contribute not only to the maintenance of international peace and security, but also to improving the whole multilateral architecture that is fit for the 21st century. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia and I give the floor to Thailand.

Co-chairs, thanks very much for holding this very important discussion. I know that it is a cliché to repeat this statement, but it's a fact that improving the Council's working method is one of the low-hanging fruits which we believe could help enhance the Council's credibility and effectiveness. On today's discussion of the working methods of the Security Council, my delegation would like to emphasize the following points. First, to strive for a more effective, credible, and accountable Council, it is Thank you very much. It is very important that we need to see political will and the Council unity. It is undeniable that the rising political tensions have made the Council more polarized and less able to take a decisive action. But to maintain the primary responsibility for the maintenance of peace and security, able to put down their differences, in particular on the issues of humanity and humanitarian adversity. Secondly, we recognize a vital role of the elected members of the Council in shaping a more productive outcome. Greater participation of the elected members should be strengthened. Independent holdership or co-penholdership. We are of the view that their role may become more significant in terms of the threshold of the affirmative votes needed to adopt a resolution, depending on how an expanded council will take shape in the future. Third, peace and security cannot be considered in silo. A multidimensional approach is crucial for tackling current global challenges.
