We therefore support increased coordination among the Council and other UN bodies, including of course the General Assembly, ECOSOC, and the Peacebuilding Commission. It is essential that these relevant bodies work in synergy in addressing geopolitical tensions and global challenges. And lastly, Thailand supports timely and more intense consultations with countries, regions, and regional organizations on the peace and security issues, including any draft resolutions that may impact them. We also look forward to enhanced consultations with troop-contributing countries with regard to mandate renewals. Co-chairs, I would like to reaffirm Thailand's commitment to working with other member states to intensify our collective efforts for the reform of the Security Council. We need to pursue and make progress not only in the working methods but all remaining clusters in tandem on the revised co-chairs' element paper. We should narrow down areas of divergence and It proposes broadened areas of convergence based on progress achieved so far within IG and in line with Actions 39 to 41 of the Pact for the Future, and it condenses with General Assembly Decision 62/557 and other relevant resolutions and decisions of the General Assembly. Our ultimate aspiration co-chairs to strengthen the United Nations and the multilateral system with the UN at the core. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Thailand and I give the floor to China.

Thank you, co-chairs. First of all, I thank you for convening today's meeting. China is about to conclude its work as Council Presidency for the month of February. In light of the experience we gained from serving as President of the Council, I would like to share my understandings and views on the issue of the Council's working methods. The Security Council is currently having quite some problems that need to be addressed in terms of both the symptoms and root causes. If underrepresentation of the Council is to be addressed as root causes, then Erroneous thinking and irrational working methods are to be rectified as symptoms. This is an essential element to improve the Council's work and make it more efficient. The Council's working methods need to keep pace with the times, function in a democratic, efficient, and transparent manner, give expression to the equal participation and shared responsibility of members, enable the Council to maximize its role and enhance the international community's confidence in and expectation of the Council. China believes we can start our work in the following areas. The first is to strengthen unity and cooperation. Among the numerous issues under the Council's working methods, Unity is the most important one. The Council belongs to the broad membership. No matter how involved and complex the challenges are, jointly maintaining international peace and security has always been our primary responsibility. Council members should respect each other, consult on an equal footing, accommodate the legitimate concerns of all parties, ensure that the Council takes timely and effective actions and that the resolutions adopted by the Council are effectively implemented. Disagreements and differences should not be intentionally aggravated, let alone creating any man-made divisions and confrontations. The second is to reform— the second is to reform the penholdership. One of the critical issues in the Council's working methods, the penholdership, is about responsibilities, not privileges. Change needs to be made in the unjust and unreasonable situation where most items on the Council's agenda have long been penned by a small number of countries. Penholders should be objective and fair, focus on coordination and consensus building, instead of being arbitrary, having double standards, and imposing on others. China supports having multiple Council members acting as co-penholders, recommends promoting the practice whereby both categories of Council members hold the pen, and supports non-permanent members in playing a bigger role. This will help the council better address hotspot issues and is conducive to maintaining the unity and a cooperative atmosphere of the council. The third is to be more open and inclusive. The countries in question, regional countries, and regional organizations usually have the best understanding of the historical context and present-day challenges of hotspot. Issues. The Security Council should give attention and listen to their voice, put ideas together, and work jointly for a solution. This is also an aspect that China is paying the most attention to during its Council presidency. We have all along endeavored to make sure that the door of the Council presidency is always open to the broad membership and to all concerned China trusts that the co-chairs will follow the mandate contained in GA Decision 62/557, take a holistic view of members' discussions around the 5 clusters of the Council's reform, and inspire all parties to engage in even more in-depth and pragmatic reflections and discussions. China would like to work together with all parties to push the ITM process to continue on the track of frank dialogue and consultation to build consensus and narrow down differences. Thank you, co-chairs.
I thank the distinguished representative of China and I give the floor to the Republic of Korea.

Thank you, Chair. I wish to thank you for convening this 3rd IGM meeting. Genuine reform should go beyond simply enlarging the Council. It must focus on improving the Council's capability and effectiveness. In this context, we believe the 2024 Presidential Note updating Presidential Note 507 on working methods is a step forward toward greater transparency and efficiency. Now, it is crucial to build on such efforts to shape a more representative and capable Council. In this regard, my delegation would like to briefly highlight the following points. First, a reformed Council must improve its working methods in a way that empowers elected members. The fact that elected members can bring diverse global perspectives through their different backgrounds and their stronger ties to the broader UN membership sets them apart from permanent members. However, based on our experience as a current elected member, We've observed that the disparities between permanent and elected members go beyond the veto power outlined in the Charter. While the veto is the most significant imbalance from the outside, in practice elected members also face less visible procedural challenges which can limit their ability to participate fully and effectively. Thus, it is important that these structural barriers are addressed in a fair and constructive manner. The UFC's reform model— longer-term non-permanent seats with the possibility of an immediate reelection— also offers a practical path to improving the Council's working methods. Indeed, the possibility of reelection would incentivize greater accountability, leading to a more sustained commitment and transparent decision-making processes. Second, the Council's working methods must be further refined to strengthen its interaction with other relevant UN bodies based on the comprehensive approach to peace. Peace is inherently a continuum spanning from conflict prevention, resolution, and peacekeeping to peacebuilding, all of which are closely intertwined. Connecting these dots is essential if the Council is to effectively fulfill its primary responsibility of maintaining international peace and security. At the same time, the Council cannot work in a silo, and collaboration with other relevant bodies, including the Peacebuilding Commission, is crucial for sustaining peace. As a member of both the PBC and the Security Council, and as the informal coordinator between the two, Korea will redouble its efforts to facilitate interactive discussions and explore concrete ways to enhance synergies between the two bodies. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Korea, and I give the floor to Estonia.

I thank the permanent representatives of Austria and Kuwait for leading the intergovernmental negotiations on the Security Council reform, and I very much welcome today's discussion on UN Security Council working methods. It appears that everyone agrees that the Security Council must be more transparent, must be more efficient, must be more inclusive in conducting its business to better respond to the current and future global threats. Where we cannot agree is whether improving the working methods is a substitute to a real comprehensive reform or not. I think that the most rational way forward is actually to push forward common understanding when it comes to comprehensive Council reform while assuring in parallel rapid progress when it comes to the working methods of the Security Council. And improving the working methods have its own merit and is absolutely indispensable if we want to make any solid progress in the short term. And indeed, there is a pressing need to improve Security Council working methods as soon as possible to ensure the Council can already now better fulfil its mandate. Towards international peace and security. We do not need to wait for the full reform to adjust and advance Security Council working methods. Therefore, we thank Japan for their tremendous work in the Security Council with updating the Note 507. It is a living document that, of course, requires continuous review, but it's a good one. Meanwhile, it is important to ensure the full participation of all members of the Security Council in its work. This includes, for example, more burden sharing among all Council members in terms of penholdership, indeed, and systematic consultations with affected countries like host countries or TCCs or PCCs. We call also for fully implementing Action 41 of the Pact for for the future, namely improving the working methods of the Council, strengthening its relationship with the General Assembly, fully implementing and adhering to all provisions of the Charter, including Article 27 of the Charter, support credible, timely, and decisive action by the Council to prevent or end the commission of genocide, crimes against humanity, or war crimes. Reinforced by the events undermining, in my view at least, the UN Charter and its principles that were unfolding this very Monday in the Security Council, let me specifically emphasize the urgent need to full and consistent implementation of Article 27 of the Charter. We call on all Council members to ensure the implementation of an obligatory abstention of a party to a dispute from voting. By the way, text of resolution adopted in the Security Council on 24th of February leaves no room for interpretation when it comes to who are the parties to the dispute in this concrete case. Finally, we sincerely believe that under the able leadership of our co-chairs, We can indeed make solid progress during the IGN session and broaden the scope of elements of consensus for the Security Council reform with a view to develop a consolidated model, preferably already by the end of the current IGN cycle. And the consolidated model should be based on the large area of convergences of the 5 clusters and the models presented by member states. as prescribed in the Pact for Our Future. And progress mentioned would help us to move directly to the text-based negotiations. And Estonia is ready to contribute its share towards these ends. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Estonia, and I give the floor to Zimbabwe.

Thank you, Co-Chair, for convening this debate. My delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by Sierra Leone on behalf of the African Group. and I'll make the following remarks in a national capacity. When our heads of state and government adopted the Pact for the Future in September 2024, they gave renewed impetus to discussions on the reform of the Security Council. It is therefore our responsibility to translate commitments made by our leaders to tangible actions that will enhance the representativeness, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, and inclusivity of the Security Council. In that regard, my delegation underscores the need to fully implement Action 41 of the Pact for the Future, which emphasizes enhanced working methods, stronger engagement between the Security Council and the General Assembly, adherence to all Charter provisions, including Article 27, and decisive action to prevent or end genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Co-chair, the Security Council cannot work in isolation if it is to achieve its mandate of promoting international peace and security. Greater coordination with the General Assembly, the Peacebuilding Commission, ECOSOC, as well as enhanced engagement with regional organizations such as the African Union and troop and police contributing countries will enhance transparency, inclusivity, inclusivity, inclusivity, and the credibility of the Council. The voices of non-Council members, regional organizations, and stakeholders must be meaningfully integrated into decision-making processes. The current system where decisions are largely predetermined before broader consultations take place must give way to a more participatory approach. Further, additional platforms such as the AREIA formula meetings promote engagement between council and council and non-council members and should remain a tool that supports our efforts towards transparency and inclusivity. Co-chair, the Pact for the Future also underscores the importance of adhering to the decision-making provisions of the UN Charter, including Article 27, which requires parties to a dispute to abstain from voting. Full implementation of this provision would prevent the misuse of the veto in situations where impartiality is needed, ensuring that Security Council decisions serve the collective interests of peace rather than geopolitical rivalries. The frequent use of the veto continues to undermine the Council's credibility and effectiveness. That is why the common Africa position, as espoused in the Ezulwini Consensus and Citi Declaration, states that while Africa is opposed in principle to the veto, so long as it exists and is a matter of justice, it should be made available to all permanent members of the Security Council. Co-Chair, the commitment to reviewing working methods including the penholder and core penholder system, is another welcome step. We commend the extension of the penholder system to members of the E10, as this promotes burden sharing and brings different political and functional capacities. The core penholdership should become the standard practice, ensuring that affected regions, particularly Africa, have a direct role in shaping decisions that impact This would not only enhance the legitimacy of the Council's work, but also improve the quality and effectiveness of its resolutions. While structural reform may take time, the penholder system and the Council's broader decision-making processes can and must be reformed immediately. The Council must also reform its sanctions regime and mandate implementation mechanisms. Sanctions, sanctions should be fair, targeted, and designed with input from the countries and regions they affect. Similarly, peacekeeping mandates must be shaped through inclusive dialogue with host countries and regional actors to ensure realistic objectives and meaningful outcomes. To conclude, let me stress that improving working methods is integral to the broader reform of the Security Council. Improving the working methods is particularly relevant in light of the geopolitical realities that often impede the Council's ability to effectively address global peace and security challenges. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe, and I give the floor to Morocco.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chair. First of all, I would like to commend the remarkable work by Mr. Alexander Maršić, the former Permanent Representative of Austria co-chairing the IGN process on the question of equitable representation on and increase in the membership of the Security Council and matters related to the Security Council. Key thematic debate on the working methods of the Security Council in the context of the intergovernmental negotiations. This is a central subject for the effectiveness and credibility of this principal organ responsible for international peace and security in carrying out its mandate. Co-chairs, for the Kingdom of Morocco, reform of the Security Council must be comprehensive and not gradual, and take into account the 5 clusters without exclusivity or exclusion, as is stipulated in Resolution 62/557. We attach a great deal of importance to effectiveness and the efficiency, as well as responsibility, in the working methods of the Security Council, and we are convinced of the need for the Council to adapt and to evolve in the face of the complex challenges in the 21st century. We underscore the importance of considering an expansion of the Security Council, not just in terms of numerical terms, but also in terms of equitable representation. In this regard, the Kingdom of Morocco considers that it is necessary to expand the Security Council in the 2 categories of membership provided for in the United Nations Charter, that is to say, permanent and non-permanent, and this in a contemporary way that better reflects the geopolitical and cultural diversity of our current world. The Kingdom of Morocco fully supports the common African position contained in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirt Declaration. My country supports just and equitable representation for Africa in the 2 categories of seats with at least 2 permanent seats with all of their prerogatives and privileges, which includes the right of veto if such continues to exist, as well as 5 non-permanent seats in order to do do justice to our continent and to repair an unconscionable and unjustified injustice done to one of the most important regional groups among the permanent members of the Security Council. Also, as an Arab country, we support greater representation of Arab countries that are heavily concerned by the issues that the Council is seized of through a permanent Arab seat with all prerogatives. As well as appropriate representation in the category of non-permanent members. Mr. Co-Chair, regarding the working methods of the Security Council, Morocco welcomes the significant progress that has been made towards a more inclusive and responsive Council. We underscore our appreciation for the continued efforts to improve the Council's working methods and practices, including through the adoption of Note 507 that has been updated As soon as they join the Council, as well as a more balanced sharing of the role of penholder, which ensures that the elected members can make an active contribution to the drafting of texts. Mr. Co-Chairs, although the number of public meetings has increased in recent years, the holding of private consultations continues to be essential in order to effectively and efficiently discuss sensitive subjects and to find compromises. These closed meetings allow for delicate issues to be addressed that require discretion and confidentiality, which are key elements in making a success of negotiations within the Council. I would also like to pay tribute to the Security Council Affairs Division for its crucial role in the continuous improvement of the Council's working methods through its activities, reports, and analyses. As well as its readiness to— its disposition vis-à-vis UN member states. We support the better restructuring of the Council's work, in particular by making the annual reports more complete by now including special reports on the use of the veto as well. Mr. Koches, as a troop-contributing country, and this since the 1960s, and a major contributor to United Nations peace efforts, The Kingdom of Morocco is in a good position to bear witness to the positive results of the actions of the Security Council for peace, security, and the peaceful settlement of disputes, particularly on the African continent. In this context, consultation meetings among the members of the Security Council and troop-contributing countries, as well as triangular meetings among the 2 aforementioned parties and the Secretariat, is a fundamental asset for the implementation of the mandates of peacekeeping operations, and it's also an effective way to strengthen transparency, cooperation, and interaction between the Security Council and United Nations member states. In this regard, we welcome the strengthening of the relationship between the Security Council and the Peacebuilding Commission, particularly when it comes to participation and contribution of the chairs of the Commission and the chairs of the country configurations to members of the Council. As well as through the advice of country configurations during the adoption of resolutions concerning member states that are on the agenda of both organs. This coordination should continue and strengthen itself in order to achieve benefits and also to strengthen the link between conflict prevention, peacekeeping, peacebuilding, and sustaining peace. As regards the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly, Thank you very much. The preservation of the institutional balance between these 2 organs is essential. The United Nations Charter is very clear as to the functions, powers, and prerogatives of each respective organ. The Security Council is designated by the United Nations Charter as being the principal organ responsible for the maintenance of international peace and security. This is a clear mandate that has no ambiguity in it. Compliance with the provisions of Article 12 for the United Nations Charter is essential for the implementation of the mandates of both organs and to avoid interference, duplication, and overlaps between their respective functions and powers. In conclusion, I would like to reiterate the Kingdom of Morocco's support to the format and the intergovernmental nature of our work. My delegation reaffirms its commitment to supporting the implementation of the reforms undertaken and to contributing alongside all member states to to a more representative Security Council that better represents the interests of all members of the United Nations. I would like to reiterate to you, co-chairs, the full support of my delegation and reiterate our determination to continue to participate constructively and positively in our work. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Kingdom of Morocco, and I give the floor to Argentina.

Good afternoon. Thank you very much. Co-chairs, distinguished Permanent Representative of Kuwait, allow me at the outset to thank on behalf of the Republic of Argentina the fact that you have organized this new— renewed meeting of the Intergovernmental Negotiations on Reform of the Security Council of the United Nations. Today we are discussing the working methods, one of the 5 clusters established by Decision 62/557 of Argentina aligns with the statement delivered by the distinguished Permanent Representative of Italy on behalf of the Uniting for Consensus Group and wishes to deliver the following comments in our national capacity. We believe that the question of the Security Council's working methods is very relevant indeed so as to improve the functioning of that organ. But what is more, to harness efforts to make it more agile and democratic. With that in mind, Argentina understands that efforts deployed by various member states over recent years are very valid and positive, but they are insufficient. It should be highlighted that in general these achievements were the outcome of efforts from elected members of the Council, and that's no coincidence because we know that a more agile, effective Council will only be achieved through a system based on greater participation of elected member states and a diminished participation of states with veto powers. Argentina believes it's totally feasible and possible to make progress towards improving the working methods of the Security Council in the short term. Given that this doesn't involve any reform of the United Nations Charter, but rather in many cases the proper implementation of what is already enforced. Historically, Argentina has defended the need to have a Security Council with working methods which are transparent, inclusive, open, democratic, and efficient. Along these lines. We are guided by our conviction that much work remains to be done when it comes to access to information, both past and present. Presentation of resolution and penholders. The election of chairs and co-chairs of the subsidiary bodies. The use of Article 27.3 of the United Nations Charter and the implications of the use of the veto. Without undermining efficiency in the Council's decision-making, we must strive to ensure that it is more transparent and democratic in how it relates to the rest of the organization's member states. And here it is very clear that we need to promote a complementary and cooperative relationship between the Council and the General Assembly with respect for the principles of the Charter in favor of international peace and security. Because of all I have just explained, Argentina favors in the context of the Uniting for Consensus negotiating group a comprehensive reform of the Council, which foresees a series of substantive improvements at every level of the Council's functioning. This is also how decision— the 2008 decision came into being, noting that in the middle of the 21st century it would be ineffective to grant to other states equal or greater prerogatives to those which are already held by the 5 permanent members. On the other hand, Argentina would like to also refer to the functioning of the sanctions committees of the Council where we're not fully aware of their implementation or their efficiency. Because of that, we believe that due process here needs to be applied. Something similar happens with referrals made by the Security Council to the International Criminal Court where the process and lack of results tend to undermine the authority of these bodies. Another aspect of the utmost importance to my country is the preparation of the annual report of the Security Council. In the context of the competencies of that body and in terms of the binding nature of its decisions, such a descriptive report is not sufficient or productive. There's a need to share information which gives account of the advantages of the decisions functioning of the Security Council. However, Argentina recognizes the progress made, particularly in terms of considering a section on the use of the veto. In sum, the Republic of Argentina is committed to improving the working methods of the Council and believes that in the end this will only be brought about by. By changing that body's culture in terms of how it adopts decisions, the efficiency of its performance, and accountability. All of this is urgent and can no longer be delayed, given that 2024 was complex for the Security Council, and that's because of the excessive use of the veto. Our country isn't in favor of such an excessive use of the veto, and so we are committed to a reform process which in the main promotes a more agile, effective, democratic UN system. We will need to work closely together to bring this into being. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Argentina. I give the floor to Australia.

Thank you, Co-Chair. Australia has consistently championed transparent and effective working methods of the Security Council. To enable the Council to start its mandate. Australia welcomes the progress made in this regard, particularly under the leadership of Japan to revise Note 507, the comprehensive compilation of working methods of the Council. Today, I wish to elaborate on 3 key ways to improve the working methods of the Council. First, Australia supports enhancing participation by briefers in the Security Council. This includes participation in Council meetings by those working in the field, often at greatest risk to their own personal safety, whether civil society representatives or humanitarian briefers. Their expertise provides valuable firsthand insights to the Council on threats to international peace and security. Second, Australia supports increasing consultation and coordination between the Security Council with other UN bodies, particularly the Peacebuilding Commission. The Commission, as per its mandate and functions, provides valuable advice to the Council on cross-cutting peacebuilding needs and priorities. This includes to assist Council decision-making on the formation, review, and drawdown of peace operations and special political mission mandates. As a current member of the Commission, Australia recognizes the need to strengthen the Commission's advisory role to the Council amid a concerning rise in armed conflict. We welcome this progress to date, including strengthened language on collaboration between the Council and the Commission in the revised Note 507 on Council working methods. But more can be done. We call for the implementation of the revised Note 507 and to explore ways for the Commission to advise the Council in a more timely manner. Third, Australia supports ongoing implementation of initiatives to improve the transparency of the Council. Especially regarding the use of the veto, like the veto initiative which Australia has championed. In this regard, we appreciated the most recent annual report of the Security Council to the General Assembly, which included for the first time a dedicated chapter on the special reports on the use of the veto. We encourage UN member states' continued participation in General Assembly debates on the use of the veto, especially the participation of States to explain their use of the veto. In summary, Australia will continue to get to engage on pragmatic ideas and proposals to strengthen the working methods of the Security Council in support of maintaining international peace and security. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia, and I give the floor to Nigeria.

Thank you, Chair, for bringing us together again on this very important discussion towards an eventual reform of the UN Security Council. My delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by the distinguished representative of Sierra Leone on behalf of the African Group and the distinguished representative of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines For the group of L69, Nigeria remains fully committed to the efforts to ensure a comprehensive reform of the United Nations system that will uphold the principles, objectives, ideals, and adherence to the values of democratization and inclusiveness, anchoring this organization on the respect for these principles as well as the promotion of common interests and inclusivity will ensure international harmony. During the High-Level Summit of the Future at the 79th UNGA session, world leaders adopted the Pact for the Future and once again called for the total overhaul of the global governance structure. Our leaders agreed to strengthen their commitment to the IGN process. In addition to the demand for Africa and the underrepresented regions to be given a just representation at the Council, in light of the prevailing global geopolitical tension and as a matter of urgency, we need to conclude this process. We agree with the representative of Saint Vincent and Grenadines that it is time. To move away from repetitive series of debates and discussions that fail to yield concrete actions, we ever wish to note as follows: The Council, as presently constituted, is deprived of valuable contributions that should be made by a diverse range of voices in its decision-making process. These contributions would have instilled the much-needed values, restored its confidence, enhanced the legitimacy of its works, as well as contributed to sustainable peace, security, and global development. A reformed and restructured Security Council should be representational, as set out in Article 24 of the Charter. The global multilateral system must ensure the participation of all sovereign states and their regional groupings in all spheres of the UN system to engender a balanced, fairer, and robust debate on global matters. The new Council should adapt working methods that will ensure transparency, efficiency, and accountability, and should take cognizance of the anticipated increase in its membership. There is also the need for the Council to refrain from applying Chapter 7 of the Charter to issues that do not pose a threat to international peace and security. It should also refrain from any recourse to the imposition of prolonged sanctions on any state which serves only in the interest of one or a few states as against the general interest of the international community. Multilateral measures may only be adopted as a last resort to enforce compliance by a state with its international obligations. In same vein, It will be imperative for the new Council to undertake a revision of its provisional rules and procedures. We must strengthen the cooperation and communication between the new Security Council and General Assembly. The annual reports and special reports of the Council to the General Assembly should be more analytical in nature, while full implementation of the decisions of the Council and the General Assembly should be carried out in accordance with the UN Charter. To further enhance accountability and transparency in the Council, there is a need for the continuous holding of open sessions, open briefings, and open debates. We also call for an open, inclusive interaction or close consultation between the Council and the regional groupings on issues affecting any of its members. As well as the region. The new Council should also enhance consultation and transparency between it and troop and police contributing countries, especially on the mandate of the Council on peacekeeping operations. Regional representation is a desideratum for a more functional and representative Council that is reflective of our current geopolitical realities. It is in light of this that we remain unequivocal in respect of Africa's demand for a reform of the UN Security Council that will ensure Africa's legitimate right to fair and equitable representation in the Council. From recent developments, the veto has become a weapon of interest. That is why Africa believes that the veto should be abolished. However, in the situation that the holders of the veto are unwilling to relinquish it, then it should be extended to all the new members in the permanent category. In conclusion, co-chairs, Nigeria is committed to strengthening regional, international, and global peace and security. We reiterate the urgent need for the reform of the Council that will be efficient, transparent, and inclusive, and have the capacity to address current global security challenges. We also join others in reiterating that text-based negotiation is an idea whose time has come. We can no longer run away from it if we must move this process forward. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative. representative of Nigeria, and I give the floor to South Africa.

Thank you, Co-Chair. South Africa aligns with the statements delivered by Sierra Leone on behalf of the Africa Group and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines on behalf of the L69, and would like to make the following additional points in our national capacity. Co-Chair, the Council's structural deficiencies have rendered it unable to shoulder its responsibility of maintaining international peace and security on behalf of the membership of the United Nations, as set out in Article 24 of the Charter of the United Nations. Its configuration has resulted in the Council reflecting a relic of the past, representing neither today's geopolitical realities nor the current membership of the United Nations. Comprehensive reform of the Security Council is a necessary step that must be guided by the principles of equity and representation. As such, in a reformed Council, its working methods must also be reinforced by these principles. The informal working group on documentation and other procedural questions plays a critical role in shaping these working methods in an expanded Council, ensuring that in spite of its size, it can function effectively and benefit from the geographically diverse range of voices that will be contained in it. Co-Chair, concerns have been raised about the— how the size of an enlarged Council will impact its efficiency and effectiveness. However, once reformed, the Informal Working Group shall continue to be the subsidiary body responsible for developing working methods that ensure the Council's effectiveness, efficiency, transparency and agility as it currently does. While the 5 clusters are inextricably linked, we note that the working methods of a reformed Council cannot be developed unless we know what the constitution of a reconfigured Security Council would be. Therefore, the discussion on working methods is second to that of the categories of membership And, as the master of its working methods, a reformed Security Council, through the Informal Working Group, will have to reflect on the most appropriate working methods for its functioning. As we delay progress, Co-Chair, on reform, skepticism continues to grow about the Council's relevance and credibility in today's world and its legitimacy as the principal organ for the maintenance of international peace and security. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa and I give the floor to Ecuador.

Thank you, Co-Chair. Various facts surrounding the Security Council meeting on the war in Ukraine held 4 days ago speak volumes as to the importance of working methods and their improvement so as to provide certainty to members of the Council and particularly the UN membership as it follows the Council's agenda with attention. Ecuador recognizes the improvements which have been introduced into the Council's working methods over recent years, which has been possible thanks to cooperation and will from all of its members. Including in the unofficial work on documentation on other procedural matters. Text incorporates, for instance, for the first time, the special reports on the use of the veto in the annual report to the General Assembly. The fact that elected members draft on situations involves— increases the involvement— their involvement in the works of the Council leads to knowledge and it can contribute to strategies of the Council to ensure that its strategies in favor of peace are more consistent. This means more transparency and more opportunities for members of the General Assembly to interact with the work of the Council. For example, the wrap-up sessions we've seen at the end of each month which allow us to address the matters approached by the Council, which should therefore be interactive. This clearly to a great degree depends on the membership, which should take advantage of these meetings and not merely settle with the holding of formal sessions despite the usual openness of rotating presidencies. Third, the transparency and responsibility of the Council towards— in terms of documentation and how this is made available to member states, this could be improved and this could be more timely. And some progress has been made in this area as reflected in the recently updated Note 507. Co-chair, often it is repeated that the Security Council has ownership of its own procedures. Article 30 of the Charter is crystal clear in that connection. Given the real challenges, the real difficulties of bringing about this reform, Its working methods are essential to ensure that this body can carry out its daily tasks in an efficient, transparent, inclusive, and effective measure— manner, particularly because its decisions have a direct impact on all UN members. And, Kocia, I'd like to conclude by congratulating you as well as the former Permanent Representative of Austria for the excellent work which you have been carrying out in the leadership you've shown in these discussions, and you can count on Ecuador's support in this endeavor. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ecuador, and I give the floor to Portugal.

Thank you, Mr. President, and I'm pleased to see you sharing this timely and important meeting and also to congratulate you for the very good job you have been doing in this important topic. Excellencies and colleagues, Portugal advocates for a more transparent, inclusive and effective Security Council. Reform must go beyond composition to improve working methods, ensuring the Council can address today's security challenges. Let me very briefly highlight 5 key priorities. First, on enhancing transparency and inclusivity. The Council must strengthen its engagement with non-members, particularly affected countries, to ensure that its decisions reflect the realities on the ground. The relationship between the Council and key UN bodies, including the GA, ECOSOC, and the PBC, must be enhanced to foster greater coherence in conflict prevention and resolution. This includes thematic discussions and field visits. The Council should also improve coordination with regional organizations such as the African Union, European Union, ASEAN and others to ensure a more effective and regionally anchored response to crises. Second, improving planning and implementation of peacekeeping mandates. Regular consultations with troop and police-contributing countries must be reinforced to ensure a more strategic and informed approach to peacekeeping mandates. Mandates must be clear, realistic, context-specific, ensuring that peacekeeping operations effectively fulfill their role to protect civilians and maintain security. Third, promoting more open and inclusive formats. Portugal supports reducing closed formats, ensuring that closed-door formats, ensuring that the Council operates with greater transparency and accountability. Civil society briefers must be protected from reprisals and their geographic balance safeguarded to ensure broader perspectives are considered. Wrap-up sessions of the Council President should be instituted institutionalized to ensure a more systematic and transparent review of each month's work. Fourth, strengthening the role of elected members. Elected members should have a greater role in drafting Council outcomes and holding penholderships, ensuring a more equitable distribution of responsibilities. My country supports ensuring that all elected members preside over the Council at least once during their term to enhance fairness and participation. Fifth and last, limiting and increasing scrutiny of the use of the veto. Portugal has been a vocal advocate for limiting the use of the veto, particularly in cases of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. We support the Franco-Mexican Declaration and the ACT Code of Conduct. Which has gained the endorsement of over 2/3 of the membership, as well as strengthening the veto initiative, which brought greater accountability to the use of the veto. We also underscored the need to fully implement Article 27 of the UN Charter, thus ensuring that Council members with a direct stake in a conflict abstain from voting on related resolutions. Excellencies and dear colleagues, Mr. Chairman, Portugal supports a more representative, effective and accountable Security Council, with improved working methods as a key pillar of reform. We remain committed to building a Council that responds to global challenges while upholding its legitimacy and credibility. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Portugal. And I give the floor to the United Kingdom.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The UK remains focused on ensuring the UN Security Council can deliver on its crucial mandate, the maintenance of international peace and security. To do that, it must be able to take action to respond to conflict, resolve disagreements, and build consensus through constructive and informed debate. All of this relies on effective and efficient Council working methods. The UK supports efforts to review, improve, and strengthen the Council's working methods and welcomes the efforts of the Council's Working Group on this issue. I will touch on 3 particular issues relating to working methods which I know are of particular interest to Members. Firstly, we recognize the General Assembly's appetite for increased transparency in the work of the Council on matters of international peace and security. As penholder of the 2023 UNSC Annual Report, we convened an informal General Assembly meeting ahead of the drafting process to garner input on how the report can best service the needs of the wider membership, engaging constructively on proposals put forward by member states. We are encouraged that an informal meeting with the wider membership took place again ahead of the drafting of the 2024 report and hope this now becomes standard practice. Second, on the question of penholding, the UK recognizes the appetite from the wider UN membership to improve this informal convention. We have worked with elected Council members as co-penholders on a variety of files and have benefited from our co-penholders' insight and expertise. More broadly, UK works closely with Council members on all files on which we penhold or co-penhold, consulting and engaging extensively. This is an approach we will continue to take. Finally, I would like to touch on the frequency of Council meetings and their conduct. The UK continues to push back against efforts to call meetings which do not have a clear purpose and artificially overload the Council's agenda. The Council's programme of work must be be sufficiently streamlined to allow it to remain agile as we face an increase in conflict around the world. And Council meetings must be focused, with competent briefers, including from civil society, civil society, who enrich, not distract from, Council discussions. Effective, efficient meetings ensure the Council can focus on delivering its core mandate. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. And I give the floor to Slovenia.

Thank you very much, Mr. Co-Chair. Slovenia has presented both its general and more detailed views on the reform several times in the past, most recently at the General Debate in the General Assembly. But since this is our first time speaking at this session of the IGN, let me briefly summarize the main points. The reform of the Security Council must be part of a broader reform of the UN. UN, and it must make the Council more efficient, effective, legitimate, democratic and responsive. More specifically, Slovenia supports the expansion of the Security Council in both categories of membership, with the aim of ensuring that the Security Council reflects today's and tomorrow's realities and changing global relations. At the same time, the reform must ensure or enhance the effectiveness of the Council's response. The Council must respond quickly and responsibly. It needs to be inclusive and representative. The fact that the UN membership has increased significantly since the last enlargement is a strong enough argument for reform and the increase of membership. Likewise is the fact that some groups are clearly underrepresented, most notably Africa, and Slovenia holds a very positive view of the African Common Position. Securing stronger and more permanent voice from the region is both a question of correcting historical injustice as well as a necessity to maintain legitimacy, credibility and relevance of the Council. Slovenia also strongly advocates for an additional non-permanent seat for the Group of Eastern European Countries. Since 1964, The membership of the Group has more than doubled. One of the reform's aims must also be to provide for equal opportunities for the membership of the regional groups to be elected. On the working methods, let me emphasize the following. First, the reform of the Security Council has to tackle the question of the working methods. They are, of course, linked to other issues. Size in particular. If the number of the Security Council is to increase, even only to low 20s, it is clear that all the current methods would not be sustainable. With increased membership, the efficient management of the day-to-day business will become even more important. As a current elected member of the Security Council, we strive to contribute towards updating and streamlining the methods that would make the work efficient and effective, which would make the process predictable and would enable the Council to react promptly, in particular in the situations of mass atrocities or the threat of it. We have seen progress in the working methods of the Council in recent years, and many of them would or could be applicable in the changed Council with increased membership. We are happy to discuss this issue further. Likewise, we have noted that elected members of the Council have, particularly in recent years, contributed significantly to drafting the Council's outcome. However, there is still a lot of space for improvement. We are supportive of the shared responsibility and fair burden sharing, as elected members have much value to add. In our view, Second, in our view, the Security Council should strengthen its engagement with the wider membership through the General Assembly, the Peacebuilding Commission, the Human Rights Council, and possibly others. PBC in particular could provide very valuable advice, including on prevention and cooperation with regional and sub-regional organizations. It can also contribute to discussions on mandates and could include common field missions. And speaking of the mandates, we believe there is still space to enhance the cooperation of the Council with the TCCs. ARIA formal meetings are a means for engagement informally with wider membership and diverse stakeholders, including civil society. We recognize its value in the reformed Council as well. And third, of course, the Council will have to strike a balance between between public and private meetings and consultations. Therefore, the members of the Council will have to make compromises and changes on how to present their position, including not having every statement read at every briefing. It is important for the Council to maintain its visibility and transparency, but they, they will have to go hand in hand with the efficiency. On another crucial point, it would be extremely important that every elected member holds the presidency of the Council at least once during their term. We would encourage an enlarged Council to continue to include civil society briefers— of course, with all the safety precautions— in its deliberations. They add a lot of value to the perspective of the issue debated. Changes in the work of the Council should be properly reflected in the methods of work of the subsidiary bodies. Co-Chair, we welcome the increased communication between the IGN co-chairs and the Chair of the IWG, and we encourage this practice to continue. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia, and I give the floor to Türkiye.

Thank you, Co-Chair. Türkiye fully aligns itself with the statement delivered by the Permanent Representative of Italy On behalf of the Uniting for Consensus Group, I would also like to make the following remarks in my national capacity. During previous IGN sessions, we have repeatedly pointed out to the necessity for the UN to be fit for purpose so that it can properly address contemporary challenges in an efficient and urgent manner. Stressing once again the strong interlinkages between the 5 clusters of General Assembly Decision We believe that in-depth deliberations on the Security Council's working methods is imperative. We therefore thank the co-chairs for convening this meeting. Today, we would like to draw attention to 4 key aspects on the working methods of the Security Council to enhance its accountability, representativeness, efficiency, transparency, and its democratic quality. First, we are increasingly witnessing the constructive role undertaken by the elected members of the Council, and we welcome their efforts. We further encourage their meaningful, equal, and active participation in decision-making processes and in all the endeavors of the Security Council. Second, we call for more equitable and balanced distribution of responsibilities and labor to ensure inclusivity in the Council especially on penholderships and chairships of subsidiary bodies along with other central tasks. Third, we remain convinced that the more transparency the Council displays while undertaking its work, the more accountable it will be. The more it shares information with non-Council Members, consults and accepts input, the more effective it will become. A more responsive Council to the UN membership will be better placed to meet the challenges of an increasingly complex world. Fourth, the coordination and cooperation between the General Assembly and the Security Council must be strengthened. The votings in the beginning of this week also displayed that the General Assembly, where all States are represented on the basis of sovereign equality, can and will continue to play a critical role regarding matters of international peace and security. We look forward to continuing our constructive engagement and further discussions. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Türkiye and I give the floor to Spain.

Muchas gracias. Thank you very much, Chair. It's always a pleasure to see you at the helm of our meetings. You can count on our full support. Thank you very much for your commitment and leadership. We would need to reform them, such as by adapting the number of votes required for a majority in line with the number of members of the council. However, while the reform—if the reform doesn't—while the reform is still pending, a number of important changes could also be. Carried out without needing to amend the UN Charter, I'd like to point some which have already been touched on by other delegations. We also believe that these are important. First, the form and content of the annual report of the Security Council. So that these can be considered by the General Assembly and more specifically the vetoes which have been used. Third, the rotating membership The rotating presidency of the Council is important and elected members should be able to take up this role the same number of times while members of the Council. Another point which has been touched on at a great deal by delegations is the link between the Peacebuilding Commission and the Security Council. We think it's very important that when advice is sought from the Peacebuilding Commission, We would therefore recall that the Uniting for Consensus model proposes increasing solely the number of elected members, which we believe are essential to improving democracy, accountability, efficiency, and representative— representativeness on the Security Council. I thank the distinguished representative of Spain, and I give the floor to Micronesia.

Thank you, Co-Chair. My credentials align with the statement delivered by the distinguished representative of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines on behalf of the group, L69 group. Co-Chairs, it is incumbent on us to address the issue of paramount importance to the future of international peace and security: the reform of the UN Security Council. We must reflect on the evolving dynamics of global governance and adapt our primary organ for maintaining peace and security to the challenges of the 21st century. The Security Council has played a pivotal role in maintaining international peace and security since its inception. However, the world has changed significantly since 1945, and the Council's, Council's working methods must evolve to reflect these changes. We must ensure that the Council remains efficient, effective, and representative of the diverse and interconnected world we inhabit today. One of the most— one of the foremost priorities in reforming of the Council is enhancing transparency and inclusivity in its decision-making process. The Security Council must be more accountable to the broader UN membership and the international community. This can be achieved through regular consultations with the UN, with the UN wider membership, regional organizations, and other relevant stakeholders. By fostering greater inclusivity, the Council can benefit from a wider range of perspectives and expertise. Leading to more informed and effective decisions. The Council's decision-making processes must be reformed to ensure timely and decisive action in response to emerging threats. We advocate for the adoption of measures that streamline the Council's procedures, reduce bureaucratic delays, and promote more efficient coordination among member states. To reflect the geopolitical realities of the 21st century, the composition of the Council must be more representative and equitable. We support the expansion of both permanent and non-permanent membership to include underrepresented regions and countries with significant contributions to international peace and security. A more inclusive Council will enhance its legitimacy and strengthen its capacity to address global challenges. Finally, the Council must enhance its cooperation with other UN organs, regional organizations, and civil society. By fostering partnership and leveraging the strengths of different actors, the Council can adopt a more holistic and comprehensive approach to conflict prevention, peacekeeping, and post-conflict reconstruction. Strengthening these synergies will enable the Council to better address the root causes of conflicts and contribute to sustainable peace. Co-chairs, the reform of the Council's working methods is essential to ensure that it remains a robust and credible guardian of international peace and security. We must seize this opportunity to adapt the Council to the realities of our time and reaffirm our collective commitments to the principles and purposes of the UN. But we run the risk of repetitive gatherings, if no real negotiations, where text-based negotiations does not commence in earnest. Let us work together to rebuild a more inclusive, transparent, and effective Council for the benefit of humankind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Micronesia. And I'll give the floor to the last speaker in our morning session. It will be Malaysia.

Thank you, Co-Chair. The debate on Security Council reform within our IGN process focuses on 5 interconnected clusters. All are essential for achieving comprehensive and sustainable reform. The Working Methods Cluster before us today is especially vital Due to its potential to transform the Council's functioning, ensuring it is inclusive, transparent, efficient, effective, democratic, and accountable. Co-chairs, for today's debate, Malaysia wishes to highlight the following 3 points. First, the Security Council holds the primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. As part of this mandate, the Council determines the priority issues that make it into its agenda. While there are instances where consensus is reached to deliberate on particular issues, there are times when this consensus is lacking. This is not always problematic, but the real concern here is when crucial issues important to the countries involved, specific regions, or particular regional groups fail to be discussed. More concerning is when the determination of the Council's agenda is subject to the narrow political interests of certain members. It is essential that the Council's agenda be shaped by the importance of issues to international peace and security, not by the political expediency of a few. Second, Malaysia supports increasing the frequency of open meetings. Where discussions and decisions are made accessible not only to Council members but also to non-members, as well as the public. This encourages transparency and accountability in the Council's work. Additionally, the expanded use of ARIA-formula meetings provides a valuable and innovative means to include non-Council members in deliberations on critical issues, offering a platform for diverse perspectives. Such practice not only enhances transparency but also fosters trust and cooperation between Council and non-Council members, contributing to a more inclusive and effective decision-making process. Third, Malaysia believes that mandating regular reporting by Council members on their actions and decisions is essential for ensuring transparency and accountability. In this regard, Malaysia commends the veto initiative introduced by Liechtenstein, adopted in 2022. Penholders play an important role in the Security Council's work, guiding the drafting of resolutions, building consensus, and facilitating negotiations among Council members to secure their adoption. Regular reporting on penholder activities is crucial, not only for accountability, but also to identify opportunities for collaboration with non-Council members, helping to advance important issues. Co-Chairs, since becoming a member of the UN, Malaysia has had the honour and responsibility of serving as an elected member of the Security Council on 4 occasions. This role is one we approach with the highest level of commitment, given the significant stakes involved. particularly in safeguarding international peace and security. In this spirit, Malaysia remains committed to contributing constructively to the work of the IGN. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia. Colleagues, we heard the last speaker for this morning. We will reconvene at 3 PM in this chamber to continue the discussion, followed by a closed interactive dialogue without webcast. Meeting is adjourned.
